cards.label: Chess
cards.learning_takeaway: Understand why checkmate ends play without capturing the king.
cards.card: Chess ends in checkmate when the opposing king is attacked and no legal move can remove the threat. The king is never actually captured. A different ending, stalemate, occurs when a player has no legal move but their king is not attacked.
cards.original_description: Exploring strategic play, tactics and positional thinking in chess.

evidence.note: Articles 1.4 and 5.2.1 support the objective, prohibition of king capture and contrasting stalemate condition; no claim that every immobile king is stalemated.

relations.note: The laws distinguish checkmate from stalemate through whether the immobile side's king is attacked.

imported_records.description: Exploring strategic play, tactics and positional thinking in chess.

cards.label: Shogi
cards.learning_takeaway: Explain the piece-reuse feature of shogi through a directly supported broad-game overview, leaving the perpetual-check exception to its separate rule card.
cards.card: Shogi is Japanese chess with a distinctive form of piece reuse. Captured pieces become reserves for their captor. Instead of moving a piece already on the board, a player can spend a turn returning a captured piece to play on their own side.
cards.original_description: Exploring Japanese chess and its distinctive piece-reuse strategies.

evidence.locator: PDF pages 1, 3 and 12, Comparisons and Placing Captured Pieces
evidence.note: Captured pieces become the captor’s reserves and may be returned to play instead of moving a board piece; no unrestricted-drop or automatic-promotion claim is used.

relations.note: The guide explicitly compares shogi with European chess and identifies returning captured pieces as a difference.

imported_records.description: Exploring Japanese chess and its distinctive piece-reuse strategies.

cards.label: Othello
cards.learning_takeaway: Understand how a placement changes ownership of intervening discs.
cards.card: Othello changes the ownership of pieces already on the board. A player places a disc to bracket an uninterrupted line of opposing discs, then flips those discs to their color. The winner has more discs when neither player can make a legal move.

evidence.note: Official outflanking and ending rules support placement, flipping and the final majority; the game need not fill all sixty-four squares.

relations.note: A lack of outflanking moves determines both forced passes and the eventual end of the game.

cards.label: Touch-move rule
cards.learning_takeaway: Understand how deliberate touching commits a player when a legal move exists.
cards.card: In over-the-board chess, a player whose turn it is normally must move the first deliberately touched own piece that has a legal move. Announcing an intention to adjust a piece before touching it is different. Clearly accidental contact does not count as deliberate selection.

evidence.note: FIDE 4.2–4.5 restricts binding touch to the player having the move, prioritizes the first legally movable own piece, and distinguishes announced adjustment and clearly accidental contact.

relations.note: FIDE's Act of Moving the Pieces regulates how a player's physical selection becomes binding.

cards.label: Threefold repetition
cards.learning_takeaway: Explain the claimable three-occurrence draw procedure, including the timing of a claim before a qualifying intended move.
cards.card: Under FIDE rules, threefold repetition permits a draw claim rather than automatically ending play. The player to move may claim when the position has appeared for the third time, or record an intended move producing it and declare that intention to the arbiter before moving.

evidence.note: FIDE 9.2.1–2 supports current-position claims and intended-move claims recorded and declared to the arbiter before execution; 9.6.1 separately supplies the automatic fivefold contrast.

relations.note: The rules distinguish a player's threefold claim from the automatic fivefold repetition draw.

cards.label: Seki
cards.learning_takeaway: Recognize mutual survival when either attack would allow the opponent to capture.
cards.card: Seki is mutual survival in Go without each group having two independent eyes. Neighboring groups share a shortage of liberties, and either player's attempt to capture can allow the opponent to capture first. Leaving the position alone therefore preserves both sides' stones.

evidence.locator: Seki: a kind of local stalemate
evidence.note: BGA's seki examples support mutual stand-off and shortage of liberties; no universal territory-scoring rule is added because rulesets differ.

relations.note: The guide introduces seki as an exception to the simple expectation that a group lacking two eyes will die.

cards.label: Komi
cards.learning_takeaway: Understand points compensating White for playing second.
cards.card: Komi compensates the player using White stones for Black's first move in Go. It adds points to White's final score rather than adding stones to the board. The British Go Association's cited default uses seven-and-a-half points; other rules or agreements can use different values.

evidence.note: BGA Default Rules gives 7½ and contrasts traditional Japanese values; How to Play explains compensation rather than placement of stones.
The guide explains compensation to White for Black moving first.

relations.note: The tournament rules identify komi as a score adjustment within Go, separately from handicap-stone placement.

cards.label: Doubling cube
cards.learning_takeaway: See how accepting a double transfers the right to offer the next redouble.
cards.card: When doubling is allowed in backgammon, a player offers it at the start of their own turn, before rolling. The opponent can decline and lose at the old value, or accept. Acceptance gives that player the cube and the exclusive right to offer the next redouble.

evidence.note: USBGF Doubling supports own-turn timing, before rolling, refusal cost and ownership. When allowed preserves format exceptions such as the separately discussed Crawford game; this is descriptive scoring, not advice to gamble.

relations.note: The federation presents the cube as the game's mechanism for offering and accepting increased stakes.

cards.label: Bearing off in backgammon
cards.learning_takeaway: Explore the conditions for removing checkers and using an oversized die roll.
cards.card: Bearing off removes checkers from a backgammon board, but only after all your active checkers reach your home board. A roll normally removes a checker from its matching point. An oversized roll can remove the highest remaining checker when no checker occupies a higher point.

evidence.note: USBGF Bearing Off supplies prerequisites and oversized-roll rule; wording avoids requiring removal when another legal move is possible.

relations.note: Bearing off is explicitly the final removal process that completes backgammon's race.

cards.label: Jacoby rule
cards.learning_takeaway: See how an optional scoring rule encourages use of the doubling cube.
cards.card: The optional Jacoby rule makes a gammon or backgammon count as a single game unless a double has been offered. It encourages use of the cube rather than waiting for a multiple-value win. The cited standard match-play rules do not use it.

evidence.locator: Optional Rules: Jacoby Rule; FAQ on match play
evidence.note: USBGF Optional Rules gives the condition and incentive; its match-play FAQ explicitly excludes Jacoby. The card preserves that format boundary instead of treating the optional convention as universal.

relations.note: The source explains Jacoby's purpose through whether players use the doubling cube during the game.

cards.label: Perpetual check in shogi
cards.learning_takeaway: Compare ordinary repetition with repeated checks that make the checking player lose.
cards.card: Repeated checking is not a safe route to a draw in shogi. Under the Japan Shogi Association's cited explanation, if continuous checks produce the same position four times, the player giving those checks loses. Ordinary repetition without continuous checking is treated differently.

evidence.locator: 連続王手の千日手というのは反則なのですか
evidence.note: The official Japanese FAQ supports the fourth-occurrence loss and distinguishes ordinary repetition; the broad Shogi card instead explains piece reuse.

relations.note: The Japan Shogi Association identifies this as shogi's special treatment of repetition by continuous check.

cards.label: Shogi impasse
cards.learning_takeaway: Explore material counting when neither advanced king can plausibly be mated.
cards.card: Under the cited professional shogi impasse procedure, both kings have entered enemy territory and neither mating prospects nor further captures remain. Rooks and bishops count five points; other nonking pieces count one. Both players having at least twenty-four points leads to a draw and replay.

evidence.locator: 持将棋の規定はどうなっていますか
evidence.note: The Japan Shogi Association FAQ specifies professional play, both kings entering enemy territory, no mating prospect or further captures, and at least 24 points each. Amateur 27-point and declaration procedures are not generalized.

relations.note: The official FAQ describes material-count adjudication as a shogi procedure and distinguishes professional from amateur variants.

cards.label: Offside in association football
cards.learning_takeaway: Distinguish occupying an offside position from committing an offside offence.
cards.card: An offside position is judged when a teammate plays or touches the ball, but position alone is not an offence. Penalization requires the specified involvement in active play. A player receiving the ball directly from a goal kick, throw-in or corner kick commits no offside offence.

evidence.note: IFAB Law 11.1–11.3 fixes the position assessment at the teammate play/touch and separately requires active involvement. Direct goal-kick, throw-in and corner-kick receipt are the stated exceptions; no exhaustive geometry or contact-point nuance is asserted.

relations.note: IFAB identifies offside as Law 11 within association football's Laws of the Game.

cards.label: Knuckleball aerodynamics
cards.learning_takeaway: Understand erratic flight from seam-dependent forces varying during the pitch.
cards.card: A baseball's seams make its surface aerodynamically uneven. As their orientation changes during flight, the effective location and direction of aerodynamic forces can vary. NASA connects these unsteady forces with the knuckleball's erratic motion, rather than explaining it solely through a steady spin-generated curve.

evidence.locator: Lift: stitches and center of pressure
evidence.note: NASA Forces on a Baseball, Lift, supports seam-dependent pressure changes and erratic motion; contrast with its separate simplified curveball model is labeled editorial in the relationship.
Steady spinning-ball trajectory is a comparison premise, not the knuckleball explanation itself.

relations.note: Contrasting seam-sensitive, time-varying forces with a regular spinning-ball model separates two different explanations of curved baseball flight.

cards.label: Tennis racket sweet spot
cards.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a low-vibration impact location from the point of maximum rebound speed.
cards.card: Physicist Rod Cross distinguishes a tennis racket's vibration-node sweet spot from its center of percussion and point of fastest rebound. An impact at the vibration node removes that component of handle motion, but rotation and translation can still transmit forces to the hand.

evidence.note: Cross sections 1 and 3 expressly separate the vibration node, center of percussion and maximum rebound, with rotation/translation/vibration components. Attribution avoids treating one terminology choice as the only sense of sweet spot.

relations.note: The source directly compares a vibration-node sweet spot with the separate center-of-percussion concept.

cards.label: Sweeping in curling
cards.learning_takeaway: Explore altering stone travel through work on the ice rather than touching the stone.
cards.card: World Curling's 2024 report describes sweepers using pressure, brush angle and technique to influence a stone's distance and curl. Athletes test methods on different ice surfaces and disagree about some effects. The account documents evolving practice rather than establishing that every reported technique works equally well.

evidence.note: The 12 January 2024 governing-body report quotes athletes about pressure, angle, surface testing and disputed knifing effects. Claims are attributed to this historical practitioner account, not certified as universal controlled findings or current equipment legality.

relations.note: The governing body's report describes sweeping as a technique within curling that changes the stone's travel through surface work.

cards.label: Appoggiatura
cards.learning_takeaway: Follow an expressive non-chord note approached by leap and resolved by step.
cards.card: An appoggiatura is a non-chord tone approached by a leap and left by a step. It is usually accented, placing the dissonance on a strong moment before resolution. The resolving step can go upward or downward; the expressive effect does not require one fixed direction.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.4 supports leap approach, step departure, usual accent and either resolution direction; maintain its analytical sense rather than every historical ornamental use of the term.
The prepared same-note approach of a suspension supports the editorial contrast.

relations.note: Both can create accented non-chord tension, but an appoggiatura arrives by leap whereas a suspension is prepared by the same note.

cards.label: Pedal point
cards.learning_takeaway: Hear a held note change harmonic status while surrounding chords move.
cards.card: A pedal point holds one note while surrounding harmonies change. It begins as a chord tone but can become a non-chord tone against later chords. Often heard in the bass, it can also appear higher up, creating continuity while its harmonic meaning shifts.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.8 supports changing harmonic status, frequent bass placement and upper-voice pedals; the card does not restrict the device to a literal organ pedal.

relations.note: Both can sustain a note across a harmonic change, but the pedal persists across harmonies while a suspension has a prepared stepwise resolution.

cards.label: Countersubject
cards.learning_takeaway: Identify recurring counterpoint accompanying successive subject entries.
cards.card: A countersubject is recurring counterpoint that accompanies a fugue's subject. Its identity matters: the composer brings back recognizable accompanying material when the subject returns, rather than inventing completely different counterpoint each time. The same countersubject can appear in different voices as the texture changes.

evidence.note: Fugue Analysis defines consistent accompaniment and identifies one countersubject in alto and soprano; no requirement that every fugue have one is imposed.

relations.note: The source defines countersubject specifically within its fugue analysis and contrasts it with nonrecurring accompaniment.

cards.label: Pitch (music)
cards.learning_takeaway: Relate perceived high and low notes to their ordering on a keyboard.
cards.card: Pitch is a sound's perceived highness or lowness. On a piano, moving right produces higher notes. For periodic musical tones, doubling the vibration frequency raises pitch by an octave, showing why musical intervals depend on frequency ratios rather than equal additions of hertz.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 1.1 supports keyboard direction; UNSW's pitch discussion supplies periodic-tone frequency and octave ratio. Keep this auditory meaning separate from material pitch.

evidence.locator: Pitch, frequency, harmonics and missing fundamental
evidence.note: Frequency ratios, including doubling for an octave, support the quantitative explanation.

relations.note: The UNSW pitch discussion explicitly uses a missing fundamental to show that perceived pitch can persist when the lowest-frequency component is absent.

cards.label: Mode locking in bowed strings
cards.learning_takeaway: See how periodic bowing can enforce harmonic motion despite inharmonic string resonances.
cards.card: A bow alternately sticks to and slips against a string, sustaining a nearly periodic motion. That nonlinear drive can pull the string's slightly mismatched resonances into harmonic frequency ratios. The resulting steady note can therefore be more harmonically regular than the freely vibrating string's natural modes.

evidence.note: UNSW explicitly attributes harmonic locking to periodic stick-slip drive; can and steady note preserve its operating-condition qualification.

relations.note: The source explains mode locking as the reason bowed motion can be harmonic despite slightly inharmonic natural resonances.

cards.label: Two Pages
cards.learning_takeaway: Explore Glass's additive process through repetitions that successively omit final notes.
cards.card: At the opening of Philip Glass's Two Pages, growth comes from adding repetitions whose final notes are progressively removed. A motive can therefore expand while newly added units become shorter. The cited analysis illustrates how repetition and subtraction can cooperate within an additive process.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 35.1 explicitly limits its Two Pages demonstration to the opening and labels the notation a transcription/analysis. The card does not assert that every section of the entire work follows the displayed process.

relations.note: The textbook analyzes the opening of Glass's Two Pages as an example of additive process, with shortening repetitions inside the expanding unit.

cards.label: Bach's Fugue in C minor, BWV 847
cards.learning_takeaway: Trace full subject entries alternating with development through fragmented motives.
cards.card: Bach's C-minor fugue from the first Well-Tempered Clavier offers a compact lesson in contrapuntal development. Its opening exposition introduces the subject in every voice. Episodes then work with smaller fragments of subjects and countersubjects, allowing recognizable material to generate passages without a complete subject statement.

evidence.note: The detailed analysis identifies first exposition, all-voice entries and fragmented material in episodes; no unsupported numerical count of voices or episodes is added.

relations.note: The source explicitly analyzes BWV 847 as a fugue with expositions and episodes.

cards.label: Bach's Invention in C major, BWV 772
cards.learning_takeaway: Recognize inversion and rhythmic augmentation within one tightly developed keyboard work.
cards.card: Bach's C-major Invention shows how a short idea can sustain development. The opening notes return with their melodic direction inverted, and fragments also appear in rhythmic augmentation. These transformations preserve recognizable material while changing its contour or the amount of time it occupies.

evidence.note: Section 11.2 identifies the first seven notes inverted later and an augmented fragment; the wording does not claim every occurrence transforms the whole theme.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly labels the invention's returning opening notes as melodic inversion.

cards.label: Adagio for Strings
cards.learning_takeaway: Hear how a 4–3 suspension delays resolution in Barber's work.
cards.card: Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings provides a textbook example of a 4–3 suspension. A prepared note becomes dissonant against the bass before resolving downward by step. The numbers describe the suspension and resolution as interval classes, so compound intervals can receive the same analytical label.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.9 labels the Barber example 4–3 and explains reduction of compound intervals in suspension labels. The revised card does not require the sounding interval to occupy a literal simple-fourth register.

relations.note: The named score example is explicitly introduced as a 4–3 suspension.

cards.label: Neapolitan chord
cards.learning_takeaway: Recognize the flattened-supertonic major chord as a chromatic predominant.
cards.card: The Neapolitan chord is a major chord built on the lowered second scale degree. In classical tonal analysis it commonly appears in first inversion and serves a predominant function. Its distinctive chromatic color therefore has a directional role, helping prepare the approach to dominant harmony.

evidence.note: Section 20.1 names flat II, most-common first inversion and predominant function; major quality follows the uppercase chord notation, not a claim that every flat-II sonority has this function.

relations.note: The Neapolitan's predominant role contrasts with the cadential six-four's dominant role, despite both often occurring near a cadence.

cards.label: Species counterpoint
cards.learning_takeaway: Learn how controlled note ratios organize practice in combining independent melodies.
cards.card: Species counterpoint teaches melodic combination through restricted rhythmic relationships. Exercises can place one, two, three or four notes against a note in another voice. The cited textbook focuses on two voices, while noting that a longer college course may extend the method to four.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 30.1 explicitly describes rhythmic ratios, its two-voice focus and up to four voices in a semester course. No uninspected claim of a staged educational or coordination benefit remains.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly presents species counterpoint as a method for learning contrapuntal composition.

cards.label: Stretch tuning
cards.learning_takeaway: Explain slightly widened piano octaves through the inharmonicity of stiff strings.
cards.card: Piano octaves are often tuned slightly wider than a strict two-to-one frequency ratio. Stiff strings have upper partials sharper than ideal harmonics. Matching the upper note to a lower string's second partial can reduce audible beating, making a mathematically exact octave a poor practical match.

evidence.note: UNSW FAQ gives stretched second partials and beat-eliminating tuning; often and can avoid prescribing one exact stretch for every piano or register.

relations.note: The FAQ explicitly explains stretched tuning as a response to stiffness-induced inharmonicity in struck piano strings.

cards.label: Just intonation
cards.learning_takeaway: Explore why pure small-ratio intervals create compromises when changing keys.
cards.card: Just intonation favors intervals described by simple frequency ratios. Yet pure fifths and pure thirds do not fit every chain of notes identically: repeated three-to-two fifths can conflict with a pure third. Fixed-pitch instruments must therefore confront compromises that adjustable voices or strings can handle differently.

evidence.locator: What is all the fuss about temperament?
evidence.note: UNSW temperament discussion supplies the chain-of-fifths mismatch and fixed versus adjustable instrument distinction; no claim that one tuning is universally best.

relations.note: The FAQ directly contrasts just intonation with meantone's compromise between thirds and fifths.

cards.label: Meantone temperament
cards.learning_takeaway: See how slightly narrowed fifths improve thirds but constrain modulation.
cards.card: Meantone temperament narrows fifths to improve the tuning of major thirds. The discrepancy is distributed across a chain of fifths rather than left entirely in the resulting third. This can suit particular keys well, while movement into other keys exposes the compromise's limits.

evidence.locator: What is all the fuss about temperament?
evidence.note: UNSW's worked example describes thirds improved by narrowing four fifths and worsening problems in other keys; no relation is made to personality temperament Q80157.

relations.note: The cited tuning comparison presents meantone as a different way to reconcile pure-interval demands on fixed-pitch instruments.

cards.label: Gradus ad Parnassum
cards.learning_takeaway: Explore Fux's historical organization of contrapuntal practice into rhythmic species.
cards.card: Johann Joseph Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum (1725) teaches contrapuntal composition through species counterpoint. The cited textbook explains this approach through one, two, three or four notes against another voice's note. The work offers a historical example of organizing musical instruction around constrained rhythmic relationships.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 30.1 gives Fux, 1725 and species pedagogy with rhythmic relationships. The revised wording does not imply that first species necessarily places a note against a longer note or claim a measured instructional outcome.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly states that Fux's work teaches composition through species counterpoint.

cards.label: Misinformation effect
cards.learning_takeaway: Explore how misleading information after an event can alter later reports.
cards.card: Later information can alter how an earlier event is remembered. In Loftus and Palmer's car-crash studies, wording in questions affected speed estimates and later reports of broken glass. The finding shows how post-event suggestions can shape reports, rather than proving that every eyewitness memory is inaccurate.

evidence.note: OpenStax describes both question wording and later glass reports; studies plural avoids treating the different experimental stages as one undifferentiated sample.

relations.note: These are different routes to memory distortion: external post-event suggestion versus confusion over a detail's source.

cards.label: Henry Molaison
cards.learning_takeaway: Compare impaired new declarative memories with preserved improvement on practiced tasks.
cards.card: Henry Molaison, known in research as H. M., had severe difficulty forming new declarative memories after brain surgery. Yet he could improve at repeatedly practiced tasks without remembering previous practice. His case separates conscious memory for an episode from learning expressed through better performance.

evidence.note: PubMed abstract of Augustinack et al. directly identifies Henry Molaison as H. M.; OpenStax 8.2 supports surgery and declarative impairment, and 8.3 supports improved performance without recalled practice. Do not claim all old memories remained intact.
Identifies H. M. and the effect of his operation on declarative memory; does not supply his full name.
Directly identifies Henry Molaison as H. M. and describes the operation causing his amnesia.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly uses H. M. to contrast impaired new episodic/semantic memory with preserved procedural learning.

cards.label: Absolute sensory threshold
cards.learning_takeaway: Interpret detection threshold as a probability under controlled conditions.
cards.card: An absolute sensory threshold is usually defined as the stimulus intensity detected on half of repeated presentations under specified conditions. It is therefore a probabilistic measurement, not a magical boundary below which detection never happens. The testing conditions matter when comparing how sensitive different observers appear.

evidence.note: OpenStax 5.1 supplies the fifty-percent criterion and controlled conditions; probabilistic interpretation follows that definition without importing unsupported exact sensitivity estimates.
Provides the decision-theoretic premise for the editorial comparison.

relations.note: A detection percentage alone does not separate available sensory information from a decision criterion; signal detection theory analyzes that distinction.

cards.label: Sensory adaptation
cards.learning_takeaway: Distinguish continuing sensory stimulation from reduced conscious notice over time.
cards.card: With prolonged stimulation, a continuing sensory input can become less noticeable even while it remains present. OpenStax describes this as sensory adaptation. The change highlights a gap between continuing stimulation and conscious experience, helping explain why an initially prominent feature of the surroundings can fade from awareness.

evidence.note: OpenStax's perception section explicitly describes reduced notice during continued stimulation; this phenomenological card does not assert a particular receptor mechanism or equate every attention lapse with adaptation.

relations.note: Reduced notice of sustained input differs from missing a visible unexpected event while concentrating on another task.

cards.label: Signal detection theory
cards.learning_takeaway: Explore detecting a target among noise when expectations and task goals influence reports.
cards.card: Signal detection theory separates sensory evidence from the criterion for reporting a signal. With evidence quality held fixed, lowering the criterion can increase both hits and false alarms; raising it can reduce both. Better sensitivity and greater willingness to answer yes are different changes.

evidence.note: Heeger’s Information and Criterion discussion and Figures 2–4 distinguish changing a criterion along one ROC from changing evidence quality. The revised card explicitly holds information fixed for the criterion tradeoff and makes no clinical recommendation.
Separates information quality and decision criterion, and shows the hit/false-alarm tradeoff.

relations.note: A fifty-percent detection threshold summarizes responses, while signal detection theory distinguishes evidence quality from the criterion behind those responses.

cards.label: Figure–ground (perception)
cards.learning_takeaway: See why a single image can reverse between an object and its background.
cards.card: Figure–ground organization separates a focal object from its background. In the familiar vase-and-faces image, the same boundary can outline a white vase or two dark faces. Changing which region counts as the figure changes what the image seems to depict.
cards.original_description: humans' ability to separate foreground from background in visual images

evidence.note: Section 5.6, figure-ground paragraph and Figure 5.25, support segmentation and the reversible vase/faces example; the card avoids claiming that segmentation must always precede recognition.

relations.note: Compare selecting an object against its background with perceptually completing an incomplete object; these are distinct operations illustrated in the same Gestalt discussion.

imported_records.description: humans' ability to separate foreground from background in visual images

cards.label: Milgram's obedience experiments
cards.learning_takeaway: Compare obedience in the original setup with changes produced by proximity and setting.
cards.card: Milgram's participants believed they were administering increasingly strong shocks when an experimenter instructed them to continue; the learner actually received none. In the original setting, many continued to the highest level. Changing the setting or bringing the learner closer reduced obedience, limiting any simple universal conclusion.

evidence.note: Section 12.4 describes the deceptive shock setup and lower continuation rates in office/proximity variants; no claim that all participants obeyed or that this settles explanations of historical atrocities.

relations.note: Milgram tests responses to an experimenter's commands, whereas Asch tests responses to a group's judgments. The comparison distinguishes authority-directed obedience from peer conformity.

cards.label: Research debriefing
cards.learning_takeaway: Understand why concealed research purposes must be explained after deceptive studies.
cards.card: Research debriefing explains a study after participation, especially when its purpose was concealed. Participants receive an honest account of the research question, the use of their data and why deception was used. The explanation helps restore information that the study deliberately withheld during the task.

evidence.note: Section 2.4 explicitly requires a full explanation after deceptive studies, including purpose, data use, reasons and further information; the card does not promise that explanation erases any harm.

relations.note: The ethics passage makes debriefing a requirement following deception and specifies the information participants should receive.

cards.label: Circumstantial moral luck
cards.learning_takeaway: Ask how unchosen situations expose people to different moral tests.
cards.card: Circumstantial moral luck concerns the unchosen situations that test a person's character. Someone placed in a brutal political environment may face choices another person never encounters. The philosophical problem is whether differing moral assessments are justified when the opportunity for wrongdoing itself depended on luck.

evidence.note: SEP's circumstantial-luck paragraph compares collaborators with imagined counterparts elsewhere; the card generalizes that structure without excusing atrocities or asserting that circumstances compel every action.

relations.note: Nagel's taxonomy in the entry expressly treats luck in one's circumstances as a kind of moral luck affecting assessment.

cards.label: No-false-lemmas condition
cards.learning_takeaway: Evaluate the proposed repair that knowledge cannot be inferred from false premises.
cards.card: The no-false-lemmas condition proposes repairing justified true belief by excluding beliefs inferred from false premises. It blocks some Gettier examples, but deceptive perceptual environments pose a further challenge. A belief can apparently be accidentally true without having been inferred from any false proposition.

evidence.note: SEP section 4 states the proposed fourth condition and noninferential counterexamples; the card does not claim the repair is accepted or sufficient.

relations.note: The entry expressly develops no false lemmas as an attempted additional condition for solving the Gettier problem, then presents objections.

cards.label: Fake-barn case
cards.learning_takeaway: Explore how a deceptive environment can undermine otherwise accurate perception.
cards.card: In the fake-barn case, Henry happens to see a real barn in a landscape full of convincing facades. His belief is true and apparently justified, yet could easily have been mistaken. The example challenges whether accurate perception alone guarantees knowledge in a systematically deceptive environment.

evidence.note: SEP section 4's Barn County passage supplies Henry, the real barn and facades; apparently and challenges preserve the evaluative character of the knowledge verdict.

relations.note: The source presents Barn County as a challenge to the no-false-lemmas repair because Henry's belief need not involve inference from a false premise.

cards.label: Two truths in Indian Buddhist philosophy
cards.learning_takeaway: Distinguish conventional and ultimate truth while recognizing that Buddhist schools interpret the distinction differently.
cards.card: Indian Buddhist discussions of two truths distinguish conventional understanding from an ultimate perspective. Ordinary language and practices operate conventionally, while ultimate analysis asks how things really are. Buddhist schools interpret both levels and their relationship differently, so the distinction does not express one uniform doctrine across traditions.

evidence.note: SEP opening differentiates conventional and ultimate perspectives and explicitly warns that the schools can be radically opposed; the card avoids attributing one settled metaphysics or historical origin to all Buddhism.

relations.note: The distinction concerns perspectives on truth and knowledge, inviting comparison with epistemology's study of cognitive success without assimilating all Buddhist schools to a single Western theory.

cards.label: Political science
cards.learning_takeaway: Examine how rules and participants' choices shape collective decisions involving government.
cards.card: Political science examines collective choices and conflicts, especially those involving government. A useful analysis asks which rules apply, what circumstances participants face and what choices they make. The same formal rule can produce different outcomes when the surrounding conditions or participants' strategies change.

evidence.note: OpenStax section 1.1 defines government-focused collective interactions and the rules/reality/choices framework; the final sentence expresses their interaction rather than a quantified causal finding.

relations.note: The chapter identifies a constitution as the most basic legal rules structuring government, one important instance of the rules its political-analysis framework examines.

imported_records.subsection: Society and social sciences / Politics / Political science and the state

cards.label: Parliament Act 1911
cards.learning_takeaway: Connect the 1909 budget conflict with replacing most Lords vetoes by delay.
cards.card: The Parliament Act 1911 followed the Lords' rejection of the 1909 budget. It replaced their veto over most Commons public bills with delay, while excluding bills extending Parliament beyond five years. The 1949 Act shortened that delay, showing how legislative power shifted between the chambers.

evidence.locator: Why were the Parliament Acts brought into force?; Bills not subject to the Parliament Acts
evidence.note: UK Parliament history and Bills not subject sections support the 1909 conflict, qualified veto reduction, exclusion of extensions beyond five years and 1949 shortening. This is not a rule for every bill or all changes to parliamentary duration.

relations.note: The official explanation sets the Act within normal Commons–Lords agreement and specifies circumstances where one chamber's consent can be bypassed.

cards.label: Money bills under the Parliament Acts
cards.learning_takeaway: Compare the Lords' restricted role over money bills with other public bills.
cards.card: Under the UK Parliament Acts, a Speaker-certified money bill can reach Royal Assent without Lords consent after a month without unamended passage. It must already have passed the Commons and reached the Lords at least a month before session-end; the Commons can direct otherwise.

evidence.locator: Bills subject to the Parliament Acts
evidence.note: The Parliamentary Counsel guidance, paragraphs 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.2, supplies certification and all timing/direction conditions; this supersedes the introductory page's misleading claim of automatic assent within a month and its absolute amendment claim.

evidence.locator: Paragraphs 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.2; 2.7 and 2.19 resolve misleading simplifications
evidence.note: Official guidance supports certification, Commons passage, session timing, a month without unamended Lords passage, Commons contrary direction and Royal Assent; not automatic enactment after a month.

relations.note: The guidance expressly identifies section 1 of the 1911 Act as the money-bill procedure and reproduces its legal conditions.

cards.label: Mixed-member proportional representation
cards.learning_takeaway: See how constituency representation combines with a party-proportional seat total.
cards.card: Mixed-member proportional representation combines constituency representatives with party-list seats intended to make overall representation proportional. In New Zealand's version, voters choose a local candidate and a party separately. The party vote largely determines each party's total seats, while electorate winners take individual constituency seats.

evidence.locator: Two votes; electorate MPs and list MPs
evidence.note: New Zealand Electoral Commission's MMP explanation supports separate votes and the overall party share; intended and largely accommodate allocation qualifications, and New Zealand's version prevents universalizing its exact rules.

relations.note: The official MMP explanation identifies the threshold as the New Zealand eligibility rule operating within this electoral system, not as a universal property of MMP.

cards.label: Amicus curiae
cards.learning_takeaway: Understand how a nonparty can contribute a brief to a court's consideration.
cards.card: In US court practice, an amicus curiae is a nonparty offering arguments or information through a brief. An interest in the case does not make the contributor a litigant. Each court's applicable rules govern when and how such outside submissions may be made.

evidence.note: Cornell defines the nonparty role and cites US Supreme Court Rule 37 and Federal Appellate Rule 29. US scope is explicit, while court-specific requirements avoid a universal permission or party-status claim.

relations.note: Compare a nonparty's rule-governed contribution with the injury-based requirements for a plaintiff's federal standing. An amicus brief does not itself give its author party status.

cards.label: Stare decisis
cards.learning_takeaway: Compare following a higher court with following one's own prior decisions.
cards.card: Stare decisis promotes consistency by directing courts to follow precedent. In the cited US account, vertical precedent comes from higher courts; horizontal precedent concerns a court's own earlier decisions. The Supreme Court can overrule its precedents, so continuity does not make every prior ruling permanent.

evidence.note: Cornell distinguishes horizontal and vertical precedent, cites the US Supreme Court’s limits on stare decisis and gives Brown as an example. The revised card does not imply lower courts may disregard binding higher-court precedent.

relations.note: Cornell explicitly uses Brown's rejection of the separate-but-equal precedent as an example showing that stare decisis is not absolute.

cards.label: Issue preclusion
cards.learning_takeaway: Distinguish relitigating a decided issue from repeating an entire claim.
cards.card: In US litigation, issue preclusion bars repeating a factual or legal issue already validly, finally and necessarily decided in an earlier proceeding. It can matter even when a later lawsuit is a different claim. The focus is the resolved issue, rather than repetition of the original action.

evidence.note: Cornell's collateral-estoppel definition and civil-procedure discussion support final and necessary determination; can matter avoids promising automatic preclusion without the jurisdiction's additional requirements.
The claim-level definition supports the stated contrast with a previously decided issue.

relations.note: The linked accounts distinguish preventing a repeated claim from preventing a repeated decision on an essential issue, while acknowledging varied uses of the term res judicata.

cards.label: Stratified sortition for citizens’ assemblies
cards.learning_takeaway: See how lottery recruitment and demographic stratification produce an intended mini-public.
cards.card: Ireland's citizens' assembly recruitment combines chance with demographic balancing. Randomly invited households may nominate an adult applicant; members are then selected using demographic information so the group broadly resembles society. The resulting mini-public is intended to be diverse, rather than simply comprising whoever volunteers first.

evidence.locator: How are members selected?; recruitment method
evidence.note: The official FAQ's recruitment paragraphs describe random household invitations, one adult nominee and stratified selection among applicants; intended and broadly avoid claiming perfect representativeness or eliminating nonresponse effects.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies stratified selection as the membership-recruitment procedure for Irish citizens' assemblies, connecting mechanism and deliberative body.

cards.label: FOIA segregability
cards.learning_takeaway: See why an exempt passage need not justify withholding the entire record.
cards.card: FOIA segregability means an exempt passage does not necessarily justify withholding an entire record. Federal agencies must consider partial disclosure and release reasonably separable nonexempt portions after redaction. The practical question is what can still be disclosed without revealing the information protected by a valid exemption.

evidence.note: 5 USC 552(a)(8)(A)(ii) and the final paragraph of (b) require reasonable segregation and partial release; reasonably and valid exemption preserve limits rather than promising every document has releasable fragments.

relations.note: The statute itself imposes partial-disclosure and segregation duties within FOIA, tying the mechanism directly to the federal records-access regime.
